However, **worker-level filtering happens AFTER the strand returns**.\n\n### The Deadlock\nIf a workspace has candidates but they are all:\n1. **Excluded** - Already attempted and failed within the race-lost TTL (30s)\n2. **Already assigned** - Assigned to other workers\n\nThen:\n1. `ExploreStrand::evaluate()` returns `StrandResult::BeadFound(candidates)` \n2. Throughput: **~1 bead per 40 minutes**\n- Same pinned workers processed **hundreds of beads** in the same period\n\n### Root Causes (from ADR-001)\n\n1. **Return-on-first-candidates deadlock** - `evaluate()` returns at first workspace with ready candidates, but unclaimable filtering happens later\n2. **Thundering herd** - All workers walk the same list in the same order, all converge on the same store\n3. **Store-layer limit bugs** - No `--limit` passed (truncates output) or `--limit 0` (returns empty)\n4. **Stale assignees are permanent** - `reopen` doesn't clear assignee; restarts\n\n## Proposed Fix Approach (Phase 5 Plan)\n\n### 5.1 Selection Correctness\n\n**Claimable-aware candidate filtering:**\n- Pass worker exclusion state into the strand's `Filters`\n- Scan large limit to `br ready --json`\n- Add boot-time `bf --version` handshake that WARNs on known-bad versions\n\n### 5.2 Stale-State Healing\n\n**Mend releases stale assignees on open beads:**\n- Extend cross-workspace mend to handle open beads with dead assignees\n- Clear assignees when the assigned worker has no live heartbeat\n\n**Claim-error taxonomy:**\n- Distinguish error from race in claim results\n- After N consecutive errors, emit ERROR telemetry and mark bead/store suspect\n\n### 5.3 Cadence and Liveness\n\n**Event-driven wakeups + jittered floor:**\n- Replace flat idle backoff (900s) with mtime/inotify watches on `.beads/issues.jsonl`\n- Jittered 60-120s polling floor\n- Found-but-excluded triggers short retry, never idle backoff\n\n**Periodic re-discovery:**\n- Re-run workspace discovery every N cycles\n- No upward traversal constraint remains\n\n### 5.4 Observability\n\n**Per-cycle scan telemetry:**\n- Workspaces visited\n- Candidates found\n- Exclusion (95th percentile)\n\nThis is a **nearest-rank** approach - it returns the actual data point at the calculated rank position.\n\n## Methods Researched\n\n### 1. Nearest-Rank Method\n**Formula:** `rank = ceil(p × N)` or `rank = floor(p × N)`\n\n**Advantages:**\n- Simple to implement\n- Always returns an actual observed value\n- Deterministic\n- No interpolation artifacts\n\n**Disadvantages:**\n- Can be coarse for small sample sizes\n- Less accurate for continuous distributions\n- Step-function behavior\n\n**Implementation:** `data[(n * percentile) / 100]`\n\n---\n\n### 2. Linear Interpolation Between Closest Ranks\n**Formula:**\n```\nh = p × (N - 1) + 1  # or h = p × N depending on convention\nrank_lower = floor(h)\nrank_upper = ceil(h)\nfraction = h - rank_lower\n\npercentile_value = data[rank_lower] + fraction × (data[rank_upper] - data[rank_lower])\n```\n\n**Advantages:**\n- More accurate for continuous data\n- Accounts for gaps between ranks proportionally\n- Industry standard for statistical software\n- Can estimate values between observed data points\n\n**Disadvantages:**\n- More complex calculation\n- Can return values not present in original data\n- Requires sorting (same as nearest-rank)\n\n**Rust Implementation Sketch:**\n```rust\nfn percentile_linear(sorted_data: &[f64], p: f64) -> f64 {\n    let n = sorted_data.len();\n    if n == 0 {\n        return 0.0;\n    }\n\n    let h = p * (n - 1) as f64;\n    let lower = h.floor() as usize;\n    let upper = h.ceil() as usize;\n    let fraction = h - lower as f64;\n\n    if lower == upper {\n        return sorted_data[lower];\n    }\n\n    sorted_data[lower] + fraction * (sorted_data[upper] - sorted_data[lower])\n}\n```\n\n---\n\n### 3. Other Methods\n- **CDF Method**: Uses empirical distribution function\n- **Weighted Percentile**: Uses weighted averaging\n- **Standard/Cleveland Method**: Variants of linear interpolation\n\n## Industry Standards\n\n### Rust Ecosystem\n\n**statrs** (https://github.com/statrs-dev/statrs)\n- Comprehensive statistical library\n- Includes order statistics and quantile functions\n- Well-tested and widely used\n\n**average** (https://crates.io/crates/average)\n- Single-pass statistics\n- Includes quantile functions\n- Supports no-std environments\n\n**ndarray-stats** (https://github.com/rust-ndarray/ndarray-stats)\n- Statistical routines for ndarray arrays\n- Provides order statistics\n\n### Other Languages\n- **Python (numpy)**: Uses linear interpolation by default\n- **Python (scipy)**: Multiple methods available, default is linear\n- **R**: Uses multiple methods (type=7 is default, linear interpolation)\n- **Excel**: PERCENTILE/PERCENTILE.EXC use linear interpolation\n\n## Recommendation\n\n**Use linear interpolation** for p95 calculation in NEEDLE for the following reasons:\n\n1. **Statistical accuracy**: Linear interpolation accounts for gaps between ranks proportionally\n2. **Industry standard**: Most statistical software (numpy, scipy, R) uses this by default\n3. **Better for small samples**: With only 20 samples, interpolation provides more accurate estimates\n4. **Latency measurement context**: We're measuring continuous time values, not discrete categories\n\nThe implementation cost is minimal (requires sorting, same as current), and the accuracy gain is significant for latency metrics where precision matters.\n\n## Implementation Plan\n\nReplace current nearest-rank implementation with linear interpolation:\n\n```rust\nfn calculate_percentile(latencies: &mut [u128], percentile: f64) -> u128 {\n    latencies.sort();\n    let n = latencies.len();\n    if n == 0 {\n        return 0;\n    }\n\n    let h = percentile * (n - lower_val)) as u128\n}\n\n// Usage:\nlet median = calculate_percentile(&mut latencies, 0.5);\nlet p95 = calculate_percentile(&mut latencies, 0.95);\n```\n\n## Sources\n\n- [Percentile - Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percentile) -
